articles.title: Caine Prize for African writing finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
articles.summary: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has also vehemently denied the allegation made in a US magazine.
articles.body:
The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.

Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.

"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.

The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.

The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies .

Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story

Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".

"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.

"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."

The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

articles.title: Oil production nears pre-Iran war levels, OPEC says
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia reports oil outputs soared to highest levels in months despite continued shipping disruptions.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has boosted crude outputs to their highest levels since before the Iran war disrupted supplies in February, triggering a global energy and shipping crisis.

An OPEC report issued on Wednesday said the world’s biggest oil exporter pumped 10.563 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude in October, up by over two million bpd from its September output.

That is the highest level since the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran in late February, when Saudi Arabia produced 10.882 million bpd.

Rising oil production by Saudi Arabia and Russia helped increase outputs for the OPEC+ group , which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and other nations including Russia.

OPEC+ pumped 41.23 million bpd in October, up by about 2.04 million bpd from September, according to its monthly report. Russia’s output increased as US President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian energy and announced an “ energy ceasefire ” between Ukraine and Russia in mid-October.

Riyadh sharply increased its production in February ahead of US and Israeli strikes on Iran .

Saudi Arabia’s reported increase in oil production “could help ease some of the inflationary pressure facing American consumers”, Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, told Al Jazeera.

“When more oil enters the global market, prices generally come under downward pressure, which can eventually translate into lower gasoline, transportation, and production costs in the United States,” he said. “However, higher Saudi production does not automatically mean lower prices at American gas stations.”

While US prices for petrol or gasoline fell below $4 a gallon for the first time in months this week, concerns over the stubbornly high cost of living drove the Democratic Party’s sweeping victories in US midterm elections last week.

Inflation has spiked since February, when it stood at 2.9 percent. Annual personal consumption expenditures (PCE) shot to a three-year high of 4.1 percent in May, when energy prices soared as the conflict closed off roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies transiting through the Strait of Hormuz.

Other producers managed to regain their supply positions, including the US.

However, the report noted a decline in imports by one of the world’s largest economies – Japan – where “crude imports fell sharply in September amid renewed disruptions to trade flows”.

The report data, while based on secondary sources, indicate that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports by using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers to bypass disruptions caused by the conflict.

“The UAE regained its position as the top supplier in September with a share of 49 percent, compared with 25 percent the previous month. The US was second with 28 percent, followed by Saudi Arabia with 14 percent,” the OPEC report noted.

The report indicated that Saudi Arabia’s exports have stabilised despite a secondary oil supply route – Saudi’s East-West Pipeline – coming under attack by Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. The Houthis, who are fighting the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government in Aden, continued to target the pipeline this week.

Shokri explained that “one reason Saudi Arabia has been able to recover some of its exports is its East-West Pipeline, which allows crude oil to move across the country to the Red Sea port of Yanbu without passing through the Strait of Hormuz”.

While no longer an OPEC member, the United Arab Emirates remains a major supplier and “has a similar advantage through its pipeline to Fujairah, located outside the strait”, he said.

“The bigger picture is that Gulf countries are learning how costly dependence on a single maritime chokepoint can be,” Shokri warned. “They are looking for ways to make their exports more resilient, but Hormuz remains too important to the global energy market to be easily bypassed.”

Oil output in October was equivalent to 97 percent of the 42.72 million bpd produced by OPEC+ in February, according to Reuters.

OPEC left its forecasts for global oil demand growth unchanged after cutting them for six straight months, and made no changes to its 2027 outlook.

The producer group expects global oil demand to rise by 2.55 million bpd next year to an average of 108.3 million bpd. It forecasts growth of 180,000 bpd in 2026.

The report also forecasted that Qatar, Canada, Brazil and Argentina will drive growth in energy-related liquids production in 2027.

The report offered an optimistic outlook for the Middle East’s economic performance in the near term.

“In 2027, the region’s economy is expected to rebound and economic activity to recover, supported by a resilient non-oil sector and robust domestic demand,” it said.

articles.summary: DNA evidence linked four grizzly bears to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras and Selah Reed near Bella Coola, British Columbia, officials said.
articles.body: Four grizzly bears have been linked through DNA evidence to a deadly attack on a mother and daughter in British Columbia, prompting Canadian wildlife officers to kill all four animals, officials announced Tuesday. The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said forensic testing conclusively linked an adult female grizzly and her three offspring to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, near Bella Coola. The bears were captured over the weekend and killed in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety, according to a Nov. 10 statement from the agency. BODY OF MISSING HIKER DISCOVERED OFF TRAIL AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE RARE DEADLY BEAR ENCOUNTER Investigators determined that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior, although officials did not elaborate on how the attack unfolded. "This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," said Insp. Jeff Tyre in a news briefing. More than a dozen conservation officers participated in the response, helping recover the victims, collect evidence and locate the bears while working in difficult terrain and weather conditions. GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL Balcarras, an art therapist, and Reed went missing after taking a walk on the Snooka West Trail near their home. Family members contacted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police after Balcarras missed a scheduled online meet-up. Investigators found her vehicle at the trailhead before recovering her body on Nov. 2 and Reed's body on Nov. 3. The agency said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a separate 2025 grizzly bear attack on a school group near Bella Coola that injured 11 people, including students and teachers. The investigation has concluded, although officials said further analysis will examine the response and circumstances surrounding the attack. articles.title: Hormuz Strait will ‘never return’ to pre-war status, Iran’s Ghalibaf says
articles.summary: Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator says Tehran is waiting for an official US response to its seven conditions.
articles.body:
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator, has told Al Jazeera that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran.

In an exclusive interview published on Wednesday, Ghalibaf said Iran and Oman reached an understanding to oversee the critical waterway as part of Tehran’s seven-point proposal to end the eight-month conflict.

“There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” he said.

Ghalibaf said Tehran provided a clear response to the US through a Qatari mediator that included its seven conditions for peace talks, adding that Iran is waiting for an official response.

“The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Iran’s conditions, as outlined by the chief negotiator, include lifting the US-imposed naval blockade and sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

He said these demands were part of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and their implementation was necessary before entering negotiations with the US.

“If America limits itself to what has been agreed upon without making excessive demands or engaging in behaviour that breeds distrust, then, naturally, reaching an agreement is possible,” he said.

“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States.”

Ghalibaf said US officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to mediate direct negotiations with Tehran during a visit to Moscow.

He warned against new US attacks against Iran, saying that US President Donald Trump will face another defeat and political pressure from the new Congress that takes office in January.

Iran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, he said, urging a sustainable deterrent capability, including military capabilities.

On the ongoing fighting in Yemen between the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for “Supporters of God”), Ghalibaf said that “no one should interfere” in it.

“If both the government in Yemen and Saudi Arabia were to ask for our help, we would certainly offer our assistance to help resolve their conflict,” he said.

Iran has previously offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group in October following a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

articles.title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo’s deadliest outbreak
articles.summary: BUNIA, Congo — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the spread of the disease.
articles.body: BUNIA, Congo — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the spread of the disease. According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo’s deadliest outbreak. The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces. The resurgence of violence in the two major hot spots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick. While Ituri accounts for nearly 70% of total cases, North Kivu has emerged as the main site of new transmission, according to Congolese Health Minister Roger Kamba. Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers. On Wednesday, World Health Organization Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus expressed concern about continuing attacks on health workers, citing two recent attacks that killed four of them. The violence disrupted already limited contact tracing in the hot spots, leaving more than 1,000 contacts lost to follow-up and three unconfirmed cases unaccounted for. “This appalling attack represents both a major humanitarian emergency and a significant setback to the response,” Ghebreyesus said. The outbreak has also affected some schools in Ituri, with more teachers contracting the disease. Two head teachers in Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, told The Associated Press they are worried about their teachers and students after losing members of staff. “Our students and the entire staff have been left traumatized. At this stage, we need psychologists to support us, as the situation is extremely difficult,” Isaac Singoma, one of the head teachers, said. Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the outbreak in Congo. The disease has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths. The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

articles.summary: Gene Simmons has reduced the asking price of his Beverly Hills mansion again, bringing the cost of the property down after several unsuccessful attempts
articles.body: Gene Simmons has reduced the asking price of his Beverly Hills mansion again, bringing the cost of the property down after several unsuccessful attempts to find a buyer. The KISS bassist, who purchased the contemporary residence in 2021, has repeatedly adjusted its price since putting it on the market. The house combines striking architecture, extensive views and luxury amenities, but its high asking price and the musician's personal expectations for a future owner have added an unusual dimension to the sale.Why Gene Simmons has slashed his Beverly Hills mansion priceThe latest reduction brought the Beverly Hills property to $11.5 million, according to Mansion Global. It reported that the mansion had undergone its sixth price cut since it was first listed for $13.995 million in April 2025. The latest adjustment represented a reduction of approximately $2.5 million from the original asking price.The repeated changes indicate how the musician has been repositioning the property in an effort to attract prospective buyers. Realtor had previously reported in February 2026 that the asking price had fallen to $12.5 million, following an earlier reduction from $13.99 million to $13.49 million in September.The successive cuts have brought the residence closer to its original purchase price, although Simmons could still potentially make a profit if the sale is completed at the current asking level.What makes the mansion different from other Beverly Hills homesThe property stands out for its contemporary architectural design and extensive use of glass, steel, oak and concrete. The residence also features solar-powered pool systems, radiant heated flooring and triple-panel windows designed to provide protection against fire and water.How did Simmons end up selling the houseSimmons bought the Beverly Hills residence for $10.5 million in 2021 through a limited liability company, according to Mansion Global. articles.title: Hegseth and staff reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pet...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.

Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.

Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach the defense secretary. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.

"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.

Rep. Gwen Moore, D-Wis., said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post .

It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honor U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal .

U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

articles.title: Kate Middleton opens up about cancer recovery, says nature became her 'sanctuary' during difficult journey; Princess of Wales reflects on good and bad days, parenting and mental health
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales, has offered a deeply personal insight into her cancer recovery, revealing how spending time in nature helped her navigate
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales, has offered a deeply personal insight into her cancer recovery, revealing how spending time in nature helped her navigate one of the most challenging periods of her life. Nearly two years after announcing that she was in remission, the royal has spoken about the emotional and physical realities of recovery, admitting that the journey comes with both good and bad days.In an interview with Country Life magazine, featured in its latest edition guest-edited by her husband, Prince William, Kate spoke about her connection with the natural world and how it shaped her perspective on health and healing.Comparing her recovery to the changing rhythms of nature, the Princess of Wales revealed that she was told during her hospital stay that getting better would not be a straightforward process."I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time. This is the same in nature. It shows us that periods of rest, reflection and renewal are equally as important as moments of growth," she said.The royal also explained that being outdoors helped her reconnect with herself during the difficult period, allowing her to find a deeper connection with her mind, body and spirit.Kate Middleton calls nature her sanctuary during cancer recoverySpeaking about the relationship between nature and healing, Kate said her personal experience had strengthened her belief in taking a holistic approach to illness and recovery."It is definitely connected, it is about listening and paying attention. What I feel really passionate about, having had first-hand experience, is approaching illness and recovery through a whole-person approach. Yes, serious illness creates a lot of physical challenges, but there is also a deeper part to all of us," she said.Describing why she finds comfort in the natural world, the Princess of Wales said nature offers a space where people can simply exist without expectations or judgement."I think that's because nature offers something unique. It doesn't ask anything of us. It doesn't judge us or expect us to perform. It simply allows us to be. It really has been my sanctuary and a place I've instinctively wanted to go," she said.Kate also spoke about how nature can provide hope during difficult periods, reminding people of their connection with the world around them. She described it as a quiet teacher that offers perspective and reassurance when life becomes challenging."Having a sense of connection, trusted people around you and places where you feel at peace can be incredibly important during difficult times," she said.She also believes that the changing nature of the environment reflects the way human beings evolve physically and emotionally."If you look at the natural world, it is hardly ever stagnant; if it is, it's rarely healthy," she said. "This has really helped me, thinking about how flow and movement can shift something inside you, whether in your body or your mind or your thoughts."Princess of Wales talks about children's mental health and parentingBeyond her own recovery, Kate discussed the importance of allowing children to experience nature and develop their creativity away from screens and technology.The mother of three, who shares Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis with Prince William, said she tries to give her children the freedom to explore rather than constantly directing what they should see or think.She also expressed concern about young people growing up in an increasingly technology-driven world and developing high levels of anxiety. According to the Princess, spending time outdoors can help children build their imagination, creativity and sense of independence.Recalling her own childhood, Kate said she enjoyed playing in streams, picking blackberries and spending time alone in her own world. Those simple experiences gave her a sense of freedom that she believes is difficult to find elsewhere.The Princess of Wales has consistently highlighted the importance of outdoor experiences, particularly for children, through her work on early childhood development.She also praised the work of charity Mind Over Mountains, which brings people together in natural surroundings while providing professional mental fitness support. In January, she joined a wellbeing and mindfulness walk in the Peak District with the organisation to understand how outdoor experiences can support mental health.Kate Middleton's cancer diagnosis and remission journeyKate revealed her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, following major abdominal surgery in January that year. In a video message, she announced that cancer had been detected and that she was undergoing preventive chemotherapy. The royal family has not publicly disclosed the type of cancer she was diagnosed with.In September 2024, she announced that she had completed her chemotherapy treatment but cautioned that her recovery and return to public duties would be gradual.In January 2025, the Princess of Wales revealed that she was in remission during a surprise visit to the Royal Marsden Hospital in London, where she had received treatment. Since then, she has occasionally spoken about the challenges of navigating life during and after cancer treatment.In 2025, Kate and Prince William became joint patrons of The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, reflecting their continued support for cancer care and research.Princess of Wales takes on Three Peaks Challenge after cancer treatmentKate has also taken on physical challenges as part of her efforts to support cancer-related causes. In 2026, she revealed that she had completed the National Three Peaks Challenge, which involves climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.The challenge involves scaling Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon. Kate described the experience as an opportunity to explore life beyond a cancer diagnosis while giving something back.In a personal message accompanying a photograph of her at the summit of Ben Nevis, she reflected on the wider impact of the disease."Every year, hundreds of thousands of people in this country hear the words no one wants to hear."Cancer doesn't just affect the body. It changes how you think and feel and profoundly affects every aspect of life. articles.title: Ole Miss students speak out after alleged racial harassment in video
articles.summary: Doorbell video captured two White students making monkey gestures and sounds outside an apartment where a group of Black students live.
articles.body:
The Black college students who were harassed by two White students at the University of Mississippi making monkey gestures and sounds outside their apartment are speaking out after the incident went viral.

The women said they were familiar with the stories of racism some faced at Ole Miss over the years — the school didn't allow its first Black student, James Meredith, until 1962, for instance — but they were not prepared for what they experienced last Friday.

Jakirya Metcalf, a freshman at Ole Miss, said she was in her apartment last Friday night when she saw the video on her Ring camera .

"We actually went outside and tried to, like, approach them and get them to explain why they did that," Metcalf told "CBS Mornings."

"One girl was like, 'I'm sorry we did that to four doors,'" Victoria Johnson, one of the roommates, said. "And mind you, we didn't see any one of those doors. It was just ours that was targeted. And she was like, 'We didn't mean any harm.'"

Metcalf and Johnson said the first person seen on the video, Aliana Kunes, apologized. But the second person, who made monkey sounds toward the camera, doubled down off-camera.

"She continued to make the gestures after the girl was apologizing," Johnson said. "It was like a slap in the face."

"I had said that I don't think they should go around because even if they go to other people's door and do that, I don't think they should do that because it's very disrespectful," Metcalf said.

Kunes apologized for her actions in a statement Tuesday.

"To the women I offended and to the Ole Miss community, I sincerely apologize," she wrote. "Before the incident on November 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race, however, I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful. I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color. I have apologized to the women and I pray they will forgive me."

Kunes voluntarily withdrew from the university after issuing the statement Tuesday.

When asked if she accepted Kunes' apology, Metcalf said she had mixed feelings.

"I feel like no matter like who we are, or if she knew our race or not, but the gestures and the voices, I feel like it still was very disrespectful," she said.

"I appreciate the apology, but I feel like it still doesn't change what happened on that Friday, because it's still hurtful and it's still devastating that someone would come to our camera and do that," Kaiyden Caldwell, another of the roommates, told "CBS Mornings."

Johnson's mother, Chiquita Laó, said she was surprised to learn Kunes withdrew from the university after Kunes said she was harassed.

"I hate to hear that because you know the children are the future, but I feel like everybody needs to be accountable," Laó said.

University officials said in a statement they are investigating the incident and have spoken with those targeted.

"The university has been and will continue providing care and resources to our students," the school said in a statement on Wednesday. "We have met with the impacted students and their families to offer support and discuss the relevant processes, and the investigation is moving forward. Student privacy laws prohibit the university from commenting on any specific student, including any potential disciplinary action."

Metcalf, Caldwell and Johnson said they plan to stay at Ole Miss and said they won't let the incident ruin their time at the school.

CBS News reached out to the two other women in the video but did not hear back.

"I want people to be mindful of their actions now," Johnson said. "So when people who would potentially experience the same situations to speak out and don't let things be swept under the rug, because this is a reality for us, and I feel like voices need to be heard."

articles.title: Judge rules Trump’s $10bn BBC defamation suit can proceed
articles.summary: The BBC denies defamation charge as Trump celebrates “huge victory” in court decision.
articles.body:
A United States judge has allowed President Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward in a blow to the state broadcaster.

The US president’s civil case alleges that the United Kingdom broadcaster deceptively edited a January 6 documentary, claiming the broadcaster acted with malice to damage his reputation.

Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump-appointed federal district judge in the Southern District of Florida, issued a 40-page ruling on Tuesday partially rejecting the United Kingdom broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case.

He ruled that Trump’s claim that the broadcaster damaged his reputation and knew or should have known the clip was misleading was “plausibly alleged”, or credible. While Kuntz’s decision moves the case forward, it did not establish whether Trump has proven those claims.

The president’s case against the BBC centres on an October 2024 documentary titled Trump: A Second Chance?

It features clips of a speech Trump made on January 6, 2021, to his supporters, allegedly directing attendees to storm the US Capitol , the seat of the US Congress, as lawmakers voted to certify former President Joe Biden’s win.

The president alleged that the documentary was selectively edited, with incorrect sequencing of two separate video and audio clips of the same speech – nearly 55 minutes apart – as well as editing the footage to make it appear that he was directly calling for violence.

The two curated clips included one section in which he told supporters to march on the Capitol, and another where he said, “Fight like hell”.

Trump has maintained that he never told his supporters to commit violence in a bid to prevent the peaceful transition of power, though he has long falsely claimed that vote-rigging cost him the 2020 race.

Trump had also said the edited sections of his speech omitted his calls for peaceful protest.

The BBC admitted the edit was misleading and apologised to Trump on November 13, 2025, a month before he filed the lawsuit. In seeking to have the case dismissed, it contended that its edits condensed a 70-minute speech, which the judge rejected.

However, the broadcaster continues to deny it defamed the president.

Following the ruling, a BBC spokesperson said, “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump called the latest ruling a “huge victory against Fake News BBC”.

After skipping his scheduled October deposition to hit the midterm campaign trail , the president faces a court-ordered December 11 deadline to testify under oath or risk having his defamation lawsuit against the BBC thrown out.

The original lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami in December 2025, sought a minimum of $5bn in damages each for alleged defamation and violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. The judge threw out the second claim on Tuesday.

The dispute over the edited speech, featured on the BBC’s Panorama show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, prompted a public relations crisis for the broadcaster, leading to the resignations of its two most senior executives.

The BBC case is one of several that Trump has privately filed against the press, as part of a wider pressure campaign targeting coverage he dislikes.

Across multiple jurisdictions, his attorneys have pursued staggering financial penalties against major news organisations and publishers.

The president is currently enmeshed in another $10bn defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it was previously dismissed. A judge dismissed the refiled suit on October 31, and Trump is appealing. Another defamation case seeks $15bn in damages from The New York Times and Penguin Random House, a book publisher.

In September, the president also moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked , though the outlets have continued fighting ongoing exclusions from Air Force One and the Oval Office.

articles.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
articles.summary: Known as the eBay of Lego, it has been down for three days and is yet to disclose what caused the shutdown.
articles.body:
Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.

BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell secondhand Lego sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.

It was originally set up by a fan, but Lego acquired it in 2019. In a homepage message, the firm said that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.

"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site has been breached or hacked, and whether any customer data was affected.

After being contacted by the BBC, Lego published the update.

BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.

Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.

She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform, after she had already paid for it.

She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.

The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues.

It is unclear if the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline.

Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft.

"Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters.

"I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me."

Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

articles.title: Welsh NHS bosses call for multi-year health funding
articles.summary: Next week Welsh ministers will unveil next year's draft spending plans for all public services.
articles.body:
Senior Welsh NHS bosses are calling on the Welsh government to provide multi-year funding settlements for health rather than relying on annual budgets.

Next week, ministers will unveil draft spending plans for all public services for the 2027-28 financial year.

The NHS accounts for almost half of the Welsh government's £27.5bn annual budget, but health leaders say one-year funding settlements can constrain long-term planning and transformation.

A Welsh government said it was "working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed".

The call comes from the Welsh NHS Alliance , formerly the Welsh NHS Confederation, ahead of evidence sessions at the Senedd's health committee on Thursday examining spending plans for 2027-28.

Tuesday's draft budget will need support from at least one opposition party to secure Senedd approval.

Talks between the Welsh government and opposition parties are ongoing.

Last week, the minority Welsh government relied on Labour support to pass adjustments to its spending plans for the next five months, including an extra £100m to help cut NHS waiting times.

In written evidence, the alliance warned that annual budgeting can make it harder to deliver long-term changes to the health service.

"There is a risk that annual planning cycles can constrain longer-term transformation, where benefits often require multi-year investment before being realised," it said.

The organisation argued ministers should prioritise spending that helps "shift Wales from a system focused on treating illness to one that creates health and wellbeing".

It added: "This requires multi-year funding certainty and transparent criteria for investment and disinvestment."

Deal agreed to end health visitor strike affecting baby appointments

Rural health board shake-up opposed as locals fight cuts to hospital beds

The alliance also cautioned against making cuts to broad service areas in isolation.

"The health and care system is highly interconnected, and reducing expenditure in one area can simply displace costs elsewhere, often into more expensive urgent and emergency care," it said.

It argued spending decisions should instead be based on "value, outcomes and whole-system impact".

The alliance added: "The NHS cannot sustainably meet future demand if resources remain concentrated predominantly at the point of crisis."

It called for more investment in primary and community care, rehabilitation, public health services and support for people with long-term conditions.

Council leaders responsible for social services, who will also give evidence to the committee, warned the sector is under "considerable pressure".

In written evidence, they said councils remain broadly confident of meeting their legal duties, but warned of growing concerns about the long-term sustainability of services if current trends continue.

Like NHS leaders, they also called for multi-year funding settlements.

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "We are working to improve services now while making the longer-term changes needed.

"That means a stronger focus on prevention, reducing health inequalities and supporting independent living, with services designed around outcomes rather than responding to demand."

articles.title: British soldier arrested and charged with rape of servicewoman in Cyprus
articles.summary: Lance Corporal Nicholas Horne serving in The Highlanders was arrested and charged in October.
articles.body:
A British soldier has been charged with the rape of a woman serving with the UK armed forces in Cyprus.

Lance Corporal Nicholas Horne, who serves in the 4th Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland – also known as The Highlanders – was charged with one count of rape on October 23, the Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) said.

He was arrested on October 19, two days after the DSCC was informed of the alleged rape of a woman serving in the British Forces Cyprus, which is part of the British Armed Forces.

Horne was remanded in custody pending a court-martial hearing.

The charge comes after an investigation by the major crime team at the DSCC - who independently investigate serious crime committed by people subject to service law in the UK and overseas.

An Army spokesperson said: "We can confirm that Lance Corporal Nicholas Horne was charged with one count of rape, contrary to section 1 of the Sexual Offences Act 2006, on 23rd October 2026, following an investigation by the Defence Serious Crime Command...

"There is no place for criminal behaviour in the Army, and we recognise the great courage it takes to come forward and report an offence.

"Anyone convicted of a sexual offence will be discharged from the service."

The UK retained two major sovereign bases in Cyprus' south and south east, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, as part of a 1960 treaty that established the island's independence and ended its status as a British colony.

articles.title: Iran designates Argentinian navy, air force as ‘terrorist organisations’
articles.summary: The move comes months after the government of Javier Milei designated Iran’s IRGC as a ‘terrorist organisation’.
articles.body:
The government of Iran has announced it will designate the naval and air forces of Argentina as “terrorist organisations”, in a tit-for-tat response to how the South American country designated its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in March.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday that it considers the two branches of the Argentinian military “terrorist organisations” by “the principle of reciprocity”. The statement does not mention Argentina’s army.

“It is evident that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government,” the statement adds.

Argentina’s foreign ministry responded with a statement of its own saying that it “categorically rejects” Iran’s designation.

“This measure is completely baseless and constitutes an unacceptable accusation,” the statement reads.

Wednesday’s back-and-forth, however, is not the first time that relations between Iran and Argentina have been strained.

Argentina blames the Iran-backed group Hezbollah for a deadly bombing attack on the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires in 1994, which killed 85 people and injured hundreds more.

The office of Argentinian President Javier Milei referenced that incident on March 31, when it issued the “terrorist” designation against the IRGC.

“President Javier Milei hopes this decision will settle a historical debt of more than 30 years with the families of the victims,” a statement from his office said at the time.

“This government is determined to bring the Argentine Republic back into alignment with Western civilization, while condemning and directly combating those who seek to destroy it.”

The decision to designate the IRGC as a “terrorist organisation” also aligned with a push under United States President Donald Trump to isolate Iran.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, and the two countries have called on international allies to support their offensive.

While many leaders in Latin America have avoided taking sides in global conflicts, Milei has positioned his government firmly behind the US and Israel.

Milei’s abrasive style has sometimes brought him into conflict with other countries in the region, including key regional economic players like Brazil.

The Argentinian leader has also revived his country’s dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, which his country refers to as Las Malvinas and claims as part of its national territory.

articles.summary: Prosecutors say David Agtsteribbe forged military records to join a veterans organization, then stole more than $81,000 to cover personal expenses.
articles.body: A man's alleged deception as a decorated combat veteran came crashing down this week after officials revealed he had actually been discharged from the military for bad conduct and accused him of bilking $81,000 from a veterans group. David Agtsteribbe, 58, of Long Island, allegedly claimed to have been awarded a Purple Heart while portraying himself as a wounded war hero. He was arrested two days before Veterans Day, the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office announced Tuesday. Prosecutors said Agtsteribbe was discharged as a private in 1988 after serving roughly one year in the military. He was court-martialed and pleaded guilty to stealing money from another soldier in 1987. EX-CIA OFFICER FOUND WITH OVER $40M IN GOLD BARS PLEADS GUILTY TO $194M FRAUD He later allegedly altered his discharge documents to portray himself with an honorable military record. The forged credentials helped him secure a position as a finance officer at a local veterans' organization, where prosecutors say he stole the group's funds to cover personal expenses. "There is something particularly despicable about fabricating a military record and claiming honors you have never earned," District Attorney Raymond A. Tierney said. "This defendant allegedly took that disgraceful deception even further. He is accused of falsely portraying himself as a war hero, infiltrating an organization for those who actually served this country and then betraying their trust by stealing their money. Our veterans earned their honors through sacrifice and service. This defendant allegedly exploited those sacrifices for his own selfish gain. It is a shameful abuse of trust, and one that we will prosecute." WHY SCAMMERS TARGET VETERANS AND HOW TO FIGHT BACK According to prosecutors, Agtsteribbe joined the Hampton Bays American Legion, an organization that supports military veterans and service members, in 2021 after allegedly falsifying his discharge papers to qualify for membership. The altered military records also included an elevated retirement status, which may have helped him obtain free health care and other privileges.Starting in 2022, Agtsteribbe allegedly transferred money from the organization's accounts into his personal checking account to cover personal expenses, including Amazon purchases, bills, a private business membership program, streaming services, travel, leisure activities, clothing and accessories. The total amount allegedly stolen was $81,798.31, prosecutors said. Prosecutors also revealed that Agtsteribbe had allegedly been applying for and obtaining memberships in other veterans organizations dating back to 2019, including the Military Order of the Purple Heart. In 2023 and 2024, Agtsteribbe allegedly submitted falsified discharge papers to the Town of Southampton in an attempt to avoid a $50 resident permit fee and obtain a handicap parking permit. articles.title: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.summary: The proposed radical overhaul of the welfare system would move under-25s off the main sickness benefits.
articles.body:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.

Alan Milburn's year-long report, which will be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, the Times reported .

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 18- to 24-year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet".

He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.

His report is expected to recommend that under-25s are no longer able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).

Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.

But many claimants would receive less under the plans, which the government is set to take forward into legislation in the new year.

Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.

Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.

Speaking to the Times about his report, Milburn said: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.

"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.

"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."

Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.

Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare reform under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.

If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.

The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch," Milburn added.

He said that currently "you've got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job".

His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, where young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.

"A deal isn't a deal unless there are potential consequences," Milburn said. "Entitlements and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin."

A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.

"But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure."

articles.title: Thousands of Kota students were promised six laddus each for Diwali; when the sweets went missing, they formed the Laddu Janta Party in one of India's weirdest protests
articles.summary: Ever heard of a ‘Ladoo protest’? Well, it happened in India recently.
articles.body: Ever heard of a ‘Ladoo protest’? Well, it happened in India recently. The country witnessed its weirdest protest ever, and no, this is not about JEE or NEET or asking for any NETA’s resignation. This weird protest took place in Kota, Rajasthan where thousands of students of Allen Career Institute, reportedly took to the streets in early November, demanding six laddus each. Yes, you read that right.What began as disappointment over a missing Diwali treat soon turned into an unusual student movement, complete with slogans, placards, Instagram reels and a political-style party called the ‘Laddu Janta Party’.For students preparing for competitive examinations, Diwali is more than just another festival. Many leave their homes and families to spend months in the coaching hub in Kota. The distribution of sweets before the Diwali break has been a festive gesture at coaching institutes.But this year, however, the expected sweetness reportedly went missing.Six laddus promised, not even one delivered?As per students, Allen had promised to give six laddus to each student before the Diwali. The expectation was that they would receive their share of sweets before leaving Kota for the festival break, which began around November 5.But as the holidays approached, the promised boxes had reportedly not reached several students. What might have otherwise been a minor administrative delay became a talking point across the institute's centres.Students began gathering outside different Allen branches, including areas around Coral Park and Supath, after their classes. Instead of the usual discussions about examination strategies, cut-offs and ranks, their demand was remarkably straightforward: where were their laddus?The protest reportedly continued for around two days, with students raising slogans and displaying placards. The unusual demand also attracted attention because of its timing. Kota, a city generally associated with the intense preparation culture surrounding engineering and medical entrance examinations, was suddenly witnessing a movement over a festive sweet.The Laddu Janta PartyThe students also took their campaign to Instagram and created a page called the Laddu Janta Party.The name gave the campaign the flavour of a political movement, with students using memes, reels, slogans and protest videos to highlight their demand. The internet quickly picked up on the unusual campaign, turning the missing laddus into a source of humour and amusement.The political-style branding was perhaps the most entertaining part of the episode. In a city where students routinely compete for academic rankings, the Laddu Janta Party offered a different kind of contest: one in which the most important issue was not securing a seat in an IIT or medical college but securing one's share of Diwali sweets.Why no laddus?The institute's explanation pointed towards logistical difficulties during the festive season.Allen director Brajesh Maheshwari reportedly said that the sudden increase in demand for sweets had made it difficult to arrange enough halwais to prepare the laddus within the required time. Preparing and packaging sweets for a large student population was not a small exercise.The institute reportedly began distributing laddus on November 5, following the protests. Students subsequently shared celebratory posts suggesting that their campaign had succeeded.Thus, the Laddu Janta Party's first major demand appeared to have received a response, even if the delay had already turned into a viral episode.When rival coaching institutes found a sweet opportunityThe story acquired another entertaining dimension when rival coaching institutes reportedly entered the picture.On Sunday, November 8, other coaching institutes were said to have organised a bhandara offering sweets and food to students. The gesture attracted attention amid the ongoing discussion around Allen's delayed Diwali distribution.For students who had been campaigning for their promised laddus, the sight of unlimited sweets being offered elsewhere made the contrast even more amusing.Was it really just about six laddus?For students living away from their families, festivals can carry an emotional significance that goes beyond celebrations and holidays. The protest was unusual, humorous and, in its own way. Instead of allowing their disappointment to remain a private complaint, students turned it into a shared campaign, gave it a name and found a way to make their voices heard.Six laddus. One party. articles.title: Ireland and Ukraine considering co-production of unmanned drones
articles.summary: The two leaders met in Dublin on Wednesday ahead of a meeting of European leaders on Thursday.
articles.body:
Ireland's Taoiseach (prime minister) and the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have indicated that they may cooperate on the production of unmanned drones.

The two leaders met in Dublin on Wednesday ahead of a meeting of European leaders on Thursday.

Speaking at a press conference, Zelensky indicated a willingness to work with the Irish government in the co-production of drones.

The taoiseach said work is ongoing between the two sides given Ukraine's expertise on drone technology and that the Irish are considering agreeing a memorandum with Ukraine on the issue.

Martin said unmanned drones could benefit the Republic of Ireland in terms of maritime security.

A major security operation is in place in the Irish capital for the meeting of the European leaders with extensive traffic disruption and delays expected in areas from Dublin airport to the city centre.

Public access is also being restricted in some parts of the city.

Zelensky also thanked Ireland for its "unwavering support" for Ukraine.

He said: "Ireland has always shown a full understanding of what's happening in Ukraine, and most importantly, of just how unjust Russia's aggression is against all of us, against Ukraine, and against normal, peaceful life, peaceful life in Europe."

He said he had briefed Martin on the war and said ending the conflict without Europe's participation would be "unjust" and "impossible".

"I'm grateful for the willingness to help Ukraine and for the support packages. All of these packages are extremely important," he said.

The taoiseach said Zelensky's visit, which is the third in a year, "showed the "enduring strength of the partnership between our two countries.

He added that "the friendship" between the Irish and Ukrainians has been "solidified" by the of Ukrainians who have made Ireland their home.

He described Russia's actions as "barbarous" and "vile".

"I once again offer my heartfelt solidarity to the people of Ukraine and my undying admiration for your unwavering resolve, resilience, and bravery."

articles.title: From Paris to DC - why offices are being turned into apartments
articles.summary: Office buildings with low occupancy rates are being transformed into flats.
articles.body:
When Roland Cubin walks you round what will eventually be a new Parisian apartment you have to use your imagination.

"Here you will be in the kitchen, and here is the bathroom," says the deputy CEO of French real estate company Groupama Immobilier.

It all sounds appealing, an upmarket flat in the west of Paris, but presently the space doesn't look like one at all. That's because it's currently a corner of one floor of a nine-storey office building called Le Diamant, where 1,800 people work.

Groupama Immobilier intends to convert the entire building into apartments. It should be the first of many such office-to-apartments conversions in the surrounding area.

We are in La Défense, the purpose-built, business district of the French capital, where the city has congregated its modern skyscrapers.

Mirroring a similar trend in places such as New York, Washington DC and London; Paris La Défense, the public development authority that runs the area, has unveiled plans to turn up to a fifth of the office buildings into housing.

Cubin leads us into what is currently a conference room in the centre of the building. It has no windows, which is indicative of a big challenge when turning offices into apartments – what to do with the large amount of space in the middle of every floor that doesn't get any natural light.

"There won't be any rooms there. Just access," says Roland Cubin, in reference to lifts and stairs.

Other issues include the need for more plumbing, and ceilings that can be too low.

Despite these challenges, there is a simple reason why there are plans for so many conversions – demand for offices in La Défense and across Paris has plummeted since the Covid-19 pandemic and the growth of homeworking.

"La Défense has a vacancy rate of 14-15% which is higher than it used to be," says Pierre-Yves Guice, CEO of Paris La Défense.

He adds that another reason for the conversion programme is the need to transform the business district from a place where the only thing people do is work.

"To retain companies in France and in Western Europe we need to diversify these office landscapes of the last century, because no-one wants to work in such an environment any longer," says Guice.

Ludovic Delaisse, CEO of the French arm of the Canadian real estate business Colliers, says that demand for office space in Paris has fallen by almost a third over the past five to six years.

He adds that office high rises will continue to be needed, but that cities need to make sure that leisure time can be enjoyed around them, such as having restaurants, bars, cinemas and gyms on their doorstep.

"People like the idea of grouping together in a centre of expertise [for work] - in tech hubs, for example. The challenge for La Défense is to be a place where you want to be, that you want to see when you leave work in the evening."

Inspiration for La Défense can come from Washington DC and New York City, where tax cuts for property developers are fuelling the largest amount of office to apartment conversions in the US. Like in Paris, this is in response to falling demand for office space since the pandemic.

A report last year found that 8,310 converted flats were in the pipeline in New York, and 6,533 in Washington.

In third place was Los Angeles on 4,322, followed by Chicago on 3,606.

"We set a goal of introducing 15,000 new residents downtown by 2028 and we are now on track to doing that," says Washington DC's deputy mayor for planning and development Nina Albert.

She says that while "there may be one or two pretty significant building demolitions… the majority are office conversions".

As in Paris, they've faced technical challenges. They've sometimes solved the natural light problem in the middle of office buildings by creating atriums – light sinks in other words – in the middle of them.

Albert adds that about "hundreds of millions of dollars of private investment" has flooded into the sector.

In addition to tax cuts, the DC Department of Buildings, part of the Council of the District of Columbia, has eased planning restrictions to make it easier for office conversion schemes to gain official approval in the US capital. It's a similar case in New York City.

In the UK, there are also tax cuts and eased planning rules for converting offices into apartments. This has led to a continuing boom in conversions. A report last year by property firm Knight Frank said that the number of such projects in London were 60% higher than pre-Covid levels.

Back in Paris, Cubin hopes that French authorities follow these examples and reduce both taxes and rules regarding conversions.

"Just how the government deals with the tax question will decide whether France will be able to convert 2% of its vacant offices or 18 to 23%," he says.

"And at the moment, when you transform a building in a way that changes its function, it is classed not as an old building that's been changed but as a new building with all the regulatory demands that go with that regarding car parking spaces, wheelchair access, fire safety and so on."

articles.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in English rivers
articles.summary: The decline has been put down to severe restrictions placed on the substances' use.
articles.body:
Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).

The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.

One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.

Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.

PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.

They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.

The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer.

As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.

The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.

Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.

"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.

There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.

The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.

The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.

The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.

"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.

One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.
